lessons.title: Adjective endings: when to add -e
lessons.summary: Decide whether an adjective needs -e, spell the -e forms correctly and recognise adjectives that never change.

blocks.text: An adjective can stand after a verb such as *zijn* (De fiets is **nieuw**) or directly before a noun (de **nieuwe** fiets). After the verb it never changes. Before a noun it usually gets the ending **-e** — and knowing when it does *not* is one of the key skills at this level.
After the verb: no ending
An adjective after *zijn*, *worden*, *blijven*, *lijken* or *vinden* never gets an ending, whatever the noun: De auto is **rood**. Het huis is **groot**. De kinderen zijn **moe**.

items.en: The soup is too hot.
The weather will turn bad tomorrow.
I think that film is really boring.
My parents always stay calm.

blocks.text: Before a noun: -e, with one exception

Before a noun the adjective gets **-e**. The one exception: **no -e** before a **singular het-word** when no definite word (de, het, deze, dit, die, dat, mijn, ons …) comes before it — so after *een*, *geen*, *elk*, *ieder*, *veel*, *weinig*, *zo'n*, or with no article at all.

headers: After a definite word (de, het, dit, mijn …)
blocks.caption: Only the singular het-word without a definite word in front loses the -e.

items.en: I've bought a new bike.
items.note: fiets is a de-word: -e

items.en: We have a new house.
items.note: het-word after een: no -e

items.en: The new house has a garden.
items.note: after het: -e

items.en: Our old house was in Zwolle.
items.note: a possessive counts as a definite word: -e

items.en: This isn't a good idea.
items.note: het idee, after geen: no -e

items.en: I like drinking cold water.
items.note: het water, no article: no -e

items.en: She drinks strong coffee every morning.
items.note: de koffie, no article: -e

blocks.text: Ask two questions. Is the noun a **singular het-word**? Is there **no definite word** (de, het, deze, dit, die, dat, mijn, jouw, ons …) in front of it? Only when both answers are yes does the adjective stay without -e.

blocks.wrong: Wij wonen in een grote huis.
blocks.right: Wij wonen in een groot huis.
blocks.why: Huis is a het-word and comes after een, so the adjective has no -e.

blocks.wrong: Ik vind ons nieuw huis mooi.
blocks.right: Ik vind ons nieuwe huis mooi.
blocks.why: Possessives such as mijn, jouw and ons count as definite words, so the adjective gets -e even before a singular het-word.

blocks.text: Spelling changes before -e
Adding -e creates an extra syllable, so the rules from *Spelling: long and short vowels* apply, exactly as in plurals.

Not every s or f turns into z or v. Words such as Frans, Engels and vals keep their s (**Franse**, **Engelse**, **valse**), and after a short vowel the consonant simply doubles (fris → **frisse**, laf → **laffe**). When in doubt, check a dictionary.
Adjectives that never change

items: Materials ending in -en: **houten**, **gouden**, **zilveren**, **wollen**, **leren**, **glazen** — een **houten** tafel, de **gouden** ring.
Other adjectives ending in -en, including many participles: **open**, **gesloten**, **gebroken**, **verlegen** — de **open** deur, een **gebroken** arm.
Some loanwords, mostly ending in a vowel: **oranje**, **roze**, **lila**, **prima**, **extra**, and also **gratis** — de **oranje** trui, een **extra** kamer, een **gratis** kaartje.
**linker** and **rechter** (left, right) never take -e and are normally written together with the noun: de **linkerhand**, het **rechteroog**.

blocks.text: Good to know

items: Words that describe the adjective, such as *heel*, *erg* and *echt* (very, really), get no ending: een **heel** mooie jurk (a very nice dress). You will often hear *een hele mooie jurk*, but in writing use heel; *een hele taart* means 'a whole cake'.
After *iets*, *niets*, *veel* and *wat* (something), the adjective gets **-s**: iets **lekkers** (something tasty), niets **nieuws** (nothing new), veel **moois** (lots of nice things).
A few fixed combinations drop the -e even after het: **het openbaar vervoer** (public transport), **het voortgezet onderwijs** (secondary education).

lessons.title: Comparatives and superlatives
lessons.summary: Compare people and things with -er … dan, (net) zo … als and the superlative -st, including the irregular forms beter, meer, minder and liever.

blocks.text: To compare two things, Dutch adds **-er** to the adjective and uses **dan** (than). To say something is 'the most', it adds **-st**. Unlike English, Dutch uses these endings even with long adjectives: *belangrijker* (more important), *het belangrijkst* (the most important).
The comparative: -er + dan
Comparative = adjective + **-er**. After an **r**, add **-der**: duur → **duurder**. To compare, use **dan**: Utrecht is **kleiner dan** Amsterdam.

The comparative follows the same spelling rules as the adjective ending -e (see *Adjective endings: when to add -e*): groot → groter, dik → dikker, braaf → braver, vies → viezer. The superlative adds -st to the unchanged basic form: grootst, dikst. After an s, only -t is added: vies → viest.
Irregular forms

rows: like to – prefer to – like most (see *Likes and preferences*)

items.nl: Jouw plan is **beter** dan het mijne.
items.en: Your plan is better than mine.

items.nl: Ik wil **meer** tijd voor mijn familie.
items.en: I want more time for my family.
He earns less than last year.
Most Dutch people have a bike.

blocks.text: When to use meer and meest

English uses *more* and *most* with long adjectives, but Dutch normally doesn't: interessanter, het belangrijkst. **Meer** and **meest** are used mainly with participles (**meer ontspannen**, de **meest gelezen** krant) and in the superlative of adjectives ending in -isch, where -st is hard to pronounce: logisch → logischer → **het meest logisch**.

blocks.wrong: Deze auto is meer duur dan die.
blocks.right: Deze auto is duurder dan die.
blocks.why: Dutch adds -er (after r: -der) instead of using meer with an adjective.

blocks.text: Comparing: dan, als and zo … als

Different: comparative + **dan** (Ik ben ouder **dan** mijn zus). Equal: **(net) zo** … **als** or **even** … **als** (Ik ben **net zo** oud **als** jij). Not equal: **niet zo** … **als** or **minder** … **dan**.

items.nl: Mijn broer is twee jaar **ouder dan** ik.
items.en: My brother is two years older than me.
items.note: Use the subject form after dan: dan ik (dan mij is common in speech).

items.en: It was more expensive than I thought.
Ghent is just as beautiful as Bruges.
He is as tall as his father.

items.nl: De film is **niet zo** spannend **als** het boek.
items.en: The film isn't as exciting as the book.

items.nl: Deze route is **minder** druk **dan** de snelweg.
items.en: This route is less busy than the motorway.

blocks.wrong: Mijn zus is groter als ik.
blocks.right: Mijn zus is groter dan ik.
blocks.why: After a comparative, standard Dutch uses dan. Groter als is very common in speech, but it counts as an error in writing and in exams; als belongs with zo … als.

blocks.text: The superlative

Superlative = adjective + **-st**. Before a noun it comes after a definite word and gets **-e**: **de grootste** stad, **het mooiste** huis, mijn **beste** vriend. Without a noun — after a verb, or describing an action — use **het** + superlative: Deze fiets is **het duurst**. Wie loopt **het hardst**? (The form with -e, *het duurste*, is also correct.)

items.nl: Amsterdam is **de grootste** stad van Nederland.
items.en: Amsterdam is the biggest city in the Netherlands.

items.nl: Dit is **het beste** restaurant van de buurt.
items.en: This is the best restaurant in the neighbourhood.

items.nl: Wie van jullie woont **het verst** weg?
items.en: Which of you lives furthest away?
I like spring best.
items.note: literally: I find spring the most beautiful

items.nl: Van de drie broers is Tim **de oudste**.
items.en: Of the three brothers, Tim is the oldest.
items.note: de oudste (broer): a noun is understood

blocks.wrong: Dit is het best restaurant van de stad.
blocks.right: Dit is het beste restaurant van de stad.
blocks.why: Before a noun the superlative always follows a definite word, so it takes the adjective ending -e.

blocks.text: Comparatives before a noun follow the normal -e rule: een **grotere** kamer, de **duurdere** fiets, but een **groter** huis (a singular het-word after een has no -e).
Useful patterns

items: **veel** + comparative = much …: Het is vandaag **veel** warmer dan gisteren.
**nog** + comparative = even …: Mijn nieuwe baan is **nog** leuker.
**steeds** + comparative = more and more: Het wordt **steeds** drukker op de weg.
**hoe** … **hoe** = the … the: **Hoe** eerder, **hoe** beter. **Hoe** meer je oefent, **hoe** beter je wordt.
**zo** … **mogelijk** = as … as possible: Kom **zo snel mogelijk**.

lessons.title: Likes and preferences
lessons.summary: Say what you like doing, prefer and like most with graag, liever and het liefst, make polite requests, and choose between houden van, leuk vinden and lekker vinden.

blocks.text: English *like* has several Dutch translations. Which one you need depends on what you like — an activity, a food, a person or a thing — and on whether you are politely asking for something.

rows: Ik **reis het liefst** met de trein.
you like the taste of something

blocks.text: graag: liking an activity

To say you like doing something, use the verb itself and add **graag**: Ik **zwem graag** (I like swimming). Graag is an adverb, not a verb: the conjugated verb keeps second place and graag follows it — after the subject when the subject comes after the verb.

items.en: I like reading crime novels.

items.nl: Mijn vader **kookt graag** voor de hele familie.
items.en: My father likes cooking for the whole family.

items.nl: In de zomer **zwem ik graag** in zee.
items.en: In summer I like swimming in the sea.
items.note: inversion: graag comes after the subject

items.en: Do you like playing tennis?
I'm happy to help you.
items.note: short pronouns such as je, het and hem come before graag

items.en: I don't like getting up early.
items.note: niet graag = don't like doing

blocks.wrong: Ik graag fiets naar mijn werk.
blocks.right: Ik fiets graag naar mijn werk.
blocks.why: Graag is not a verb. The conjugated verb fiets takes second place and graag follows it.

blocks.text: liever and het liefst
**Liever** (rather, prefer) is the comparative of graag, and **het liefst** (most of all) is its superlative. They go in the same place as graag. To compare two things, use **liever … dan**.

items.en: I prefer tea to coffee.

items.nl: Zullen we gaan wandelen? – Nee, ik blijf **liever** thuis.
items.en: Shall we go for a walk? – No, I'd rather stay at home.

items.nl: In het weekend slaap ik **het liefst** lang uit.
items.en: At the weekend, what I like most is a long lie-in.
What's your favourite food?
items.note: literally: what do you most like to eat?

items.en: I'd rather not.

blocks.wrong: Ik woon liever in de stad als op het platteland.
blocks.right: Ik woon liever in de stad dan op het platteland.
blocks.why: Liever is a comparative, so the comparison word is dan, just as after groter or beter.

blocks.text: Polite requests with graag

Graag also makes requests polite. *Ik wil graag …* is the standard way to order or ask for something; *Ik zou graag … willen* is even more polite. On its own, *graag* means 'please' or 'with pleasure'.

items.nl: Ik **wil graag** twee kaartjes voor de voorstelling van acht uur.
items.en: I'd like two tickets for the eight o'clock show.
I would like to make an appointment.
A cappuccino, please.
Would you like some more coffee? – Yes, please!
Thanks! – You're welcome.

blocks.text: houden van, leuk vinden, lekker vinden

items: **houden van** + noun or infinitive: to love, to be very fond of. It always needs **van**: Ik **hou van** Italiaans eten. Hij **houdt van** wandelen. Ik **hou van** je. (Ik houd and ik hou are both correct; hou is more common in speech.)
**leuk vinden**: to like, to find fun or nice. What you like is the object: Ik **vind** dit liedje **leuk**. **Vind** je het **leuk** om te dansen? Note: *Ik vind hem leuk* often means 'I fancy him'.
**lekker vinden**: to like food and drink: Ik **vind** spruitjes niet **lekker**. Lekker is also used for pleasant feelings: Het is **lekker** weer.
**mooi vinden**: to like the look of something: Ik **vind** die jas **mooi**.

blocks.text: For things, *van* + *het* becomes **ervan**: Hou je van jazz? – Ja, ik **hou ervan**. Never say *ik hou van het*.

blocks.why: In the meaning 'love, like', houden always needs van. Without van, houden means 'keep' or 'hold'.

blocks.text: In Belgium **Ik zie je graag** is the usual way to say 'I love you'. In the Netherlands people say *Ik hou van je*.

lessons.title: Separable verbs
lessons.summary: Recognise separable verbs and put the prefix in the right place in main clauses, subordinate clauses, with modals, in the perfect tense and with om … te.

blocks.text: Many Dutch verbs consist of a prefix and a verb: *opbellen* (op + bellen, to phone), *meenemen* (mee + nemen, to take along), *aankomen* (aan + komen, to arrive). In some sentences the prefix splits off from the verb and moves to the end.
In a main clause in the present or simple past — including questions and commands — the verb takes its normal place and the **prefix goes to the end of the clause**: Ik **bel** je morgen **op**.

items.en: I'll call you tonight.
The train arrives at 9.15.
Are you taking an umbrella?
Yesterday we went out with colleagues.
items.note: simple past of uitgaan

items.en: Tidy your room!
items.note: imperative

blocks.text: When the verb stays in one piece

Whenever the verb itself stands at the end of the clause, it is **one word** again: as an infinitive (after a modal, *gaan* or *zullen*), as the verb of a subordinate clause, and as a participle. In the participle, **ge-** goes between prefix and verb (op**ge**beld); with **te**, te goes between them (op **te** bellen).

rows: I want to call you tomorrow.
Ik beloof dat ik je morgen **opbel**.
I promise that I'll call you tomorrow.
Ik heb geen tijd om je **op te bellen**.
I don't have time to call you.

items.nl: De trein is tien minuten te laat **aangekomen**.
items.en: The train arrived ten minutes late.
Did you bring your passport?

items.nl: Weet jij hoe laat de winkel **opengaat**?
items.en: Do you know what time the shop opens?
items.note: subordinate clause: one word

items.nl: Ik vind het moeilijk om vroeg **op te staan**.
items.en: I find it hard to get up early.

items.nl: We gaan morgen de hele dag **schoonmaken**.
items.en: We're going to clean all day tomorrow.

blocks.why: In a main clause only the verb part goes to second position; the prefix goes to the end of the clause.

blocks.wrong: Ik weet dat de bus om acht uur komt aan.
blocks.right: Ik weet dat de bus om acht uur aankomt.
blocks.why: In a subordinate clause the verb goes to the end and stays in one piece.
In the participle of a separable verb, ge- goes between the prefix and the verb: op + ge + ruimd.

blocks.text: Recognising separable verbs

Separable verbs are stressed on the prefix: **op**bellen, **mee**nemen, **aan**komen. Verbs with the unstressed prefixes *be-*, *ge-*, *her-*, *ont-*, *ver-* and *er-* never separate: Ik **betaal**. Ik **vertel** een verhaal. Ik **ontmoet** haar morgen.

items: **aan**: aankomen (arrive), aanzetten (switch on), aantrekken (put on)
**af**: afspreken (arrange to meet), afwassen (do the dishes), afmaken (finish)
**in**: instappen (get in, get on), invullen (fill in), inpakken (pack)
**mee**: meenemen (take along), meegaan (go along), meedoen (take part)
**op**: opbellen (phone), opstaan (get up), opruimen (tidy up)
**uit**: uitgaan (go out), uitnodigen (invite), uitstappen (get out, get off)
**terug**: terugkomen (come back), terugbellen (call back), teruggeven (give back)
**weg**: weggaan (leave), weggooien (throw away)
**voor**: voorstellen (introduce, suggest), voorlezen (read aloud)
**door**: doorgaan (go on, go ahead), doorlopen (keep walking)
also: **schoon**maken (clean), **thuis**blijven (stay at home), **langs**komen (drop by), **tegen**komen (run into), **binnen**komen (come in)

blocks.text: A few verbs exist in both kinds, with different stress and meaning: **voor**komen (occur) is separable — Dat **komt** vaak **voor**. voor**ko**men (prevent) is not — Dit **voorkomt** problemen.
Word order details

items: Objects, time words and **niet** all come before the prefix: Ik bel je vanavond **niet op**.
A prepositional phrase may follow the prefix, which is very common: Ik nodig je **uit** voor mijn verjaardag. (Ik nodig je voor mijn verjaardag **uit** is also correct.)
In a subordinate clause with a modal, the prefix can also stand before the modal: … omdat ik je wil **opbellen** / omdat ik je **op** wil bellen.
If the verb part itself begins with be-, ver- etc., the participle has no ge-: voorbereiden → **voorbereid**, afbetalen → **afbetaald**.

lessons.title: Reflexive verbs
lessons.summary: Use the reflexive pronouns me, je, zich and ons with reflexive verbs, place them correctly, and tell always-reflexive verbs from sometimes-reflexive ones.

blocks.text: A reflexive verb has an object that refers back to the subject: the person does something to himself or herself. Dutch dictionaries list these verbs with **zich**: *zich wassen* (to wash), *zich vergissen* (to be mistaken). Many verbs that are not reflexive in English are reflexive in Dutch.

blocks.caption: In formal writing you may also see mij after ik. After u, both zich and u are correct (u is more usual in Belgium). After jullie, je is normal; jullie also occurs.

blocks.text: The reflexive pronoun always matches the subject: **me**, **je**, **zich**, **ons**, **je**, **zich**. **Zich** is only for the third person (hij, zij, het, ze) and u — never for ik, jij, wij or jullie.

items.en: I'm not feeling well today.
How are you feeling?
items.note: the first je is the subject, the second the reflexive pronoun

items.nl: We moeten **ons haasten**, anders missen we de trein.
items.en: We have to hurry, or we'll miss the train.

items.nl: Mijn dochter **verveelt zich** in de vakantie.
items.en: My daughter gets bored in the holidays.
Do you still remember my name?

blocks.text: Where does the reflexive pronoun go?

The reflexive pronoun comes **right after the conjugated verb**. If the subject comes after the verb (inversion, questions), the pronoun follows the subject. In a subordinate clause it comes right after the subject. **Niet** comes after the reflexive pronoun.

items.en: I shave every morning.
Every morning I shave.
items.note: inversion: verb – subject – reflexive pronoun

items.en: You shouldn't be ashamed.
I made a mistake.
items.note: reflexive verbs always take hebben in the perfect

items.en: I think he's mistaken.
items.note: subordinate clause: right after the subject

items.en: She gets dressed quickly.
items.note: separable reflexive verb: zich aankleden

blocks.why: The conjugated verb voel must be in second place; the reflexive pronoun follows it.

blocks.text: Always reflexive
Some verbs only exist with a reflexive pronoun. You cannot leave the pronoun out or replace it with another object.

rows: Ik vraag **me** af of hij komt.

blocks.wrong: Ik herinner die vakantie nog goed.
blocks.right: Ik herinner me die vakantie nog goed.
blocks.why: Zich herinneren (to remember) is always reflexive, even though English 'remember' is not.

blocks.text: Sometimes reflexive
Other verbs can be reflexive or take an ordinary object. Use **zich** when the subject does it to himself or herself, and **hem**, **haar** or a noun when it is someone or something else.

items.en: She's washing (herself).
She's washing the car.
He's getting dressed.
He's dressing his little boy.
May I introduce myself?
I'll introduce you to my mother.

blocks.wrong: Hij wast hem elke ochtend met koud water.
blocks.right: Hij wast zich elke ochtend met koud water.
blocks.why: Hem refers to another man. To say he washes himself, use the reflexive pronoun zich.

blocks.text: **zich voelen** describes how you feel: Ik voel **me** goed / moe / ziek. Hoe voelt u **zich**? Without a reflexive pronoun, voelen means 'to feel' with your hands or body: Voel eens hoe zacht dit is.
For emphasis, or after a preposition, use the -zelf forms **mezelf**, **jezelf**, **zichzelf**, **onszelf**: Hij denkt alleen aan **zichzelf**. Ik zag **mezelf** in de spiegel.

lessons.title: Perfect tense: regular participles
lessons.summary: Form the perfect tense of regular verbs with hebben or zijn and a correctly spelled past participle such as gewerkt, gewoond, gepraat or betaald.

blocks.text: The perfect tense (*de voltooid tegenwoordige tijd*) is the most common way to talk about the past in everyday Dutch: *Ik heb gewerkt* can mean 'I worked', 'I have worked' or 'I did work'. It has two parts: a form of **hebben** or **zijn**, and a **past participle** (*het voltooid deelwoord*).

**hebben** or **zijn** (conjugated, in second place) + … + **past participle** (at the end of the clause). Most verbs take hebben; which verbs take zijn is explained in *Perfect tense: hebben or zijn?*.

blocks.caption: When jij/je comes after the verb, the -t drops: Heb jij …? Ben je …?

items.en: I worked until six yesterday.
Have you called your mother yet?
We lived in Leiden for ten years.

items.nl: Mijn zus **is** vorig jaar naar Gent **verhuisd**.
items.en: My sister moved to Ghent last year.

blocks.text: Forming the participle: ge- + stem + t/d

Regular participle = **ge** + **stem** + **-t** or **-d**. The stem is the ik-form (werken → werk, maken → maak, stoppen → stop). Add **-t** if the stem ends in one of the consonants of **'t kofschip** (t, k, f, s, ch, p); otherwise add **-d**.

*'t kofschip* (a kind of sailing ship) contains every consonant that takes -t: t, k, f, s, ch, p. Some learners prefer *soft ketchup*, which has the same consonants. You can't hear the difference between -t and -d at the end of a word, so this rule is about spelling.
Watch out: v and z in the infinitive

Look at the **infinitive**, not at the written stem. If the infinitive has **v** or **z**, the participle gets **-d**, even though the stem is written with f or s: leven → leef → **geleefd**, reizen → reis → **gereisd**.

blocks.caption: Compare fietsen → gefietst and blaffen → geblaft: there the infinitive itself has s or f, so the ending is -t.

blocks.text: Stems ending in t or d

If the stem already ends in **t** or **d**, nothing is added: a Dutch word never ends in -tt or -dd. praten → **gepraat**, wachten → **gewacht**, zetten → **gezet**, branden → **gebrand**, antwoorden → **geantwoord**.
No ge- after an unstressed prefix

Verbs that begin with the unstressed prefixes **be-, ge-, her-, ont-, ver-** or **er-** get no extra ge-: betalen → **betaald**, vertalen → **vertaald**, herhalen → **herhaald**, ontmoeten → **ontmoet**, gebruiken → **gebruikt**, erkennen → **erkend**.

items.en: Have you paid the bill yet?

items.nl: Ik heb de nieuwe buren gisteren **ontmoet**.
items.en: I met the new neighbours yesterday.
items.note: stem ontmoet already ends in t

items.en: What happened?
items.note: gebeuren takes zijn

items.nl: Hij heeft dat verhaal al drie keer **verteld**.
items.en: He has already told that story three times.
Did you answer his question?
items.note: be- + antwoord: no ge-, no extra d

items.en: I cycled all weekend.

blocks.text: Separable verbs put ge- after the stressed prefix: opbellen → **opgebeld**, uitnodigen → **uitgenodigd** (see *Separable verbs*). New verbs borrowed from English follow the same rules: appen → **geappt**, chatten → **gechat**, googelen → **gegoogeld**.
Word order

The participle closes the main clause; objects, time words and **niet** come before it: Ik heb hem gisteren **niet** gebeld. In a subordinate clause both verbs stand at the end, in either order: … omdat ik hard **gewerkt heb** / **heb gewerkt** (see *Subordinate clauses: verb at the end*).

blocks.wrong: We hebben zaterdag de hele dag gefietsd.
blocks.right: We hebben zaterdag de hele dag gefietst.
blocks.why: The stem fiets ends in s, one of the 't kofschip consonants, so the participle ends in -t.

blocks.wrong: Hij heeft tien jaar in Spanje geleeft.
blocks.right: Hij heeft tien jaar in Spanje geleefd.
blocks.why: The infinitive leven has a v, which is not in 't kofschip, so the participle ends in -d.
Verbs beginning with be-, ver-, ont-, her-, ge- or er- never get an extra ge-.

lessons.title: Perfect tense: irregular participles
lessons.summary: Use the most common strong and irregular past participles, such as geschreven, gedronken, gehad and gebracht, including those of prefixed and separable verbs.

blocks.text: Many of the most frequent Dutch verbs are **strong** (*sterke werkwoorden*): their participle ends in **-en** instead of -t or -d, and often has a different vowel: schrijven → geschreven. A few others are fully **irregular**. No rule tells you which verbs are strong, so learn each one together with its participle.

Strong participle = **ge** + stem (often with a vowel change) + **-en**. The ge- rules are the same as for regular verbs: no ge- after be-, ge-, her-, ont-, ver- and er- (begrijpen → **begrepen**, vergeten → **vergeten**), and ge- in the middle of separable verbs (opstaan → op**ge**staan).
Strong verbs: common patterns

rows: lezen → **gelezen**, eten → **gegeten**, geven → **gegeven**, slapen → **geslapen**, komen → **gekomen**, lopen → **gelopen**, vallen → **gevallen**, laten → **gelaten**, zien → **gezien**
schrijven → **geschreven**, blijven → **gebleven**, kijken → **gekeken**, krijgen → **gekregen**, rijden → **gereden**, begrijpen → **begrepen**
kiezen → **gekozen**, vliegen → **gevlogen**, bieden → **geboden**, verliezen → **verloren**, sluiten → **gesloten**, ruiken → **geroken**
drinken → **gedronken**, vinden → **gevonden**, beginnen → **begonnen**, zingen → **gezongen**, winnen → **gewonnen**, helpen → **geholpen**, sterven → **gestorven**, trekken → **getrokken**
blocks.caption: Note eten → gegeten, with an extra g (also opeten → opgegeten).

items.nl: Ik heb gisteren een lange brief **geschreven**.
items.en: I wrote a long letter yesterday.
Have you read that book yet?

items.nl: We hebben in een Surinaams restaurant **gegeten**.
items.en: We ate at a Surinamese restaurant.

items.nl: Wat heb je voor je verjaardag **gekregen**?
items.en: What did you get for your birthday?

items.nl: Ze is drie dagen in Gent **gebleven**.
items.en: She stayed in Ghent for three days.
I've found my wallet!

blocks.text: Irregular and mixed verbs
Brengen, denken, kopen and zoeken form a group: all four participles end in **-cht** (gebracht, gedacht, gekocht, gezocht), and so do their simple past forms (bracht, dacht, kocht, zocht).

Some verbs mix the two types. Zeggen and vragen have regular participles (**gezegd**, **gevraagd**) but an irregular simple past (zei, vroeg). Lachen, bakken and wassen do the opposite: a regular simple past (lachte, bakte, waste) but a strong participle (**gelachen**, **gebakken**, **gewassen**).

blocks.wrong: Ik heb een nieuwe jas gekoopt.
blocks.right: Ik heb een nieuwe jas gekocht.
blocks.why: Kopen is irregular: gekocht, like gebracht, gedacht and gezocht.

blocks.wrong: Ze heeft een lange e-mail geschrijfd.
blocks.right: Ze heeft een lange e-mail geschreven.
blocks.why: Schrijven is strong: the participle ends in -en and the vowel changes from ij to e.
The participle of eten has an extra g: gegeten.

blocks.text: Prefixed and separable verbs

A verb with a prefix has the same participle as its base verb, plus the prefix: komen → gekomen, so aankomen → **aangekomen**; schrijven → geschreven, so beschrijven → **beschreven** and opschrijven → **opgeschreven**.

items.en: I got up at seven.
items.note: opstaan

items.en: Did you bring your passport?
items.note: meenemen

items.en: He ate the whole plateful.
items.note: opeten

items.en: I thought about it for a long time.
items.note: nadenken

items.nl: De trein is om tien uur **vertrokken**.
items.en: The train left at ten.
items.note: vertrekken: no ge-

items.en: Have you had breakfast yet?
items.note: ontbijten: no ge-

items.en: I've forgotten his name.
items.note: participle = infinitive

blocks.text: Learn strong verbs in threes — infinitive, simple past, participle: schrijven – schreef – geschreven, drinken – dronk – gedronken. The past forms are covered in *Simple past: irregular verbs*. Several of these verbs (gaan, komen, blijven, worden, beginnen, vallen, sterven) take zijn: see *Perfect tense: hebben or zijn?*.

lessons.title: Perfect tense: hebben or zijn?
lessons.summary: Choose correctly between hebben and zijn in the perfect tense, including verbs of motion with and without a destination.

blocks.text: Every perfect tense needs an auxiliary verb: **hebben** or **zijn**. Most verbs take hebben. A smaller but very frequent group takes zijn. The choice depends on meaning, not on whether the participle is regular or irregular.

Use **hebben** for most verbs — including verbs with a direct object and all reflexive verbs. Use **zijn** when the verb expresses a **change of place** (with a destination or direction) or a **change of state**, and with *zijn*, *blijven* and *gebeuren*.
Verbs that take zijn

rows: gaan, komen, vertrekken, aankomen, vallen, weggaan, terugkomen, binnenkomen, opstaan, verhuizen
worden, sterven, overlijden, groeien, beginnen, ophouden, stoppen (met), trouwen, veranderen, slagen, zakken, lukken

items.en: My grandfather died last year.
Haven't you grown!
The lesson has already started.
They got married in June.
Have you ever been to Maastricht?
I passed my driving test!
I managed it! / It worked!

blocks.why: Gebeuren always takes zijn in the perfect tense.

blocks.wrong: Hij heeft een week ziek geweest.
blocks.right: Hij is een week ziek geweest.
blocks.why: The verb zijn itself takes zijn in the perfect: ik ben geweest, hij is geweest.

blocks.text: Movement: with or without a destination

Verbs that describe a **way of moving** — fietsen, lopen, rijden, wandelen, rennen, zwemmen, vliegen, varen, reizen — take **hebben** when you only describe the activity, and **zijn** when you say where the movement goes (a destination or direction).

Watch the difference between place and destination: We **hebben** **in** het park gewandeld (in the park: where it happened → hebben). We **zijn** **naar** het park gewandeld (to the park: destination → zijn). Words such as *naar binnen*, *naar boven*, *terug* and *weg* also show direction: Hij **is** naar boven **gerend**.

blocks.wrong: Hij heeft gisteren naar Utrecht gefietst.
blocks.right: Hij is gisteren naar Utrecht gefietst.
blocks.why: Naar Utrecht is a destination, so the motion verb fietsen takes zijn.

blocks.text: Same verb, two auxiliaries

Some verbs can be used with or without a direct object. With an object they take **hebben**; without one they take **zijn** when they express a change. Exceptions: *beginnen* and *vergeten* keep zijn even with an object (Ik **ben** een nieuwe cursus **begonnen**).

items.en: I drove to the station.

items.nl: Ik **heb** mijn moeder naar het station **gereden**.
items.en: I drove my mother to the station.
items.note: direct object (mijn moeder) → hebben

items.en: I've stopped smoking.
The police stopped the car.
You haven't changed at all.
I've changed my plans.

blocks.why: Reflexive verbs always take hebben in the perfect tense (see *Reflexive verbs*).

blocks.text: Quick test: did the subject end up somewhere else, or become something different? → zijn. Is it just an activity? → hebben. When in doubt, choose hebben: it is right for the large majority of verbs.
**Vergeten** usually takes zijn: Ik **ben** mijn tas **vergeten**. Hebben is possible when you have put something out of your mind for good: Ik **heb** die ruzie allang **vergeten**.

lessons.title: Simple past: regular verbs
lessons.summary: Form the simple past of regular verbs with -te(n) or -de(n), including the spelling of the stem and stems ending in t or d.

blocks.text: The simple past (*de onvoltooid verleden tijd*) is a single verb form: *Ik werkte* (I worked, I was working). Dutch uses it mainly for stories, descriptions and habits in the past — see *Perfect or simple past?*. Regular verbs (*zwakke werkwoorden*) form it with **-te** or **-de**.
Simple past = **stem + -te** (singular) / **-ten** (plural) if the stem ends in a consonant of **'t kofschip** (t, k, f, s, ch, p); otherwise **stem + -de** / **-den**.

blocks.caption: Only two forms: singular and plural. There is no extra -t for jij, u or hij.

items.nl: Vroeger **werkte** mijn vader in de haven van Rotterdam.
items.en: My father used to work in the port of Rotterdam.

items.nl: Toen we in Leiden **woonden**, **fietsten** we elke dag naar de universiteit.
items.en: When we lived in Leiden, we cycled to the university every day.
It rained the whole holiday.
Did you hear that?
Grandma made pancakes every Sunday.

blocks.text: Shortcut: the simple past uses the same t or d as the participle. gewerkt → werk**te**, gewoond → woon**de**, gereisd → reis**de** (see *Perfect tense: regular participles*).
Spelling of the stem
The stem is the ik-form, with the usual spelling rules: maken → maak, stoppen → stop. The ending is simply added to it — write *maakte*, not *makte*, and *stopte*, not *stoppte*.
v and z: look at the infinitive

When the infinitive has **v** or **z**, the stem is written with f or s, but the ending is still **-de(n)**: leven → leef → **leefde**, reizen → reis → **reisde**, verhuizen → **verhuisde**, geloven → **geloofde**. Compare fietsen → **fietste**: there the infinitive itself has an s.

blocks.wrong: Ze reiste vorig jaar door Zuid-Amerika.
blocks.right: Ze reisde vorig jaar door Zuid-Amerika.
blocks.why: The infinitive reizen has a z, so the ending is -de, even though the stem is written reis.

blocks.text: Stems ending in t or d

Here you write **both** letters: a stem ending in t + -te gives **-tte**, a stem ending in d + -de gives **-dde**: praten → **praatte**, wachten → **wachtte**, antwoorden → **antwoordde**, branden → **brandde**. The participles never double: gepraat, geantwoord.

blocks.caption: You hear only one t or d, but you write two. Wij zetten is both present and past; the context tells you which.

blocks.wrong: Hij praate de hele avond over zijn werk.
blocks.right: Hij praatte de hele avond over zijn werk.
blocks.why: The stem praat ends in t, and t is in 't kofschip, so -te is added: praat + te = praatte.

blocks.text: Prefixes, separable verbs and word order

items: The simple past is one word in second position; nothing goes to the end: Gisteren **werkte** ik thuis.
Verbs with be-, ge-, her-, ont-, ver- or er- simply keep their prefix: betalen → **betaalde**, vertellen → **vertelde**, gebruiken → **gebruikte**, herhalen → **herhaalde**.
Separable verbs split in a main clause, just as in the present: Ik **belde** haar gisteren **op**. In a subordinate clause they are one word: … toen ik haar **opbelde**.
Lachen, bakken and wassen have a regular simple past but a strong participle: lachte – **gelachen**, bakte – **gebakken**, waste – **gewassen**.
Some very common verbs have an irregular simple past, for example zeggen → **zei**, vragen → **vroeg**, kopen → **kocht**: see *Simple past: irregular verbs*.

blocks.why: With a plural subject (wij, jullie, zij) the simple past ends in -ten or -den.

blocks.wrong: Gisteren werkde ik tot acht uur.
blocks.right: Gisteren werkte ik tot acht uur.
blocks.why: The stem werk ends in k, a 't kofschip consonant, so the ending is -te.

lessons.title: Simple past: irregular verbs
lessons.summary: Use the simple past of the most common strong and irregular verbs, including the vowel and spelling changes between singular and plural.

blocks.text: Many of the most frequent Dutch verbs do not form the simple past with -de or -te (see *Simple past: regular verbs*). Instead, they change the vowel of the stem: *schrijven* → *schreef*, *lopen* → *liep*. These are called **strong verbs**. A small group of very common verbs is completely irregular, such as *zijn* → *was* and *hebben* → *had*.

A strong or irregular simple past has only **two forms**: a singular form for ik, jij, u, hij, zij and het, with **no ending**, and a plural form for wij, jullie and zij, with **-en**: ik **liep**, wij **liepen**. No -t is ever added for jij, u or hij.

blocks.caption: One form for the singular, one for the plural

items.nl: Gisteren **schreef** ik een lange mail aan mijn baas.
items.en: Yesterday I wrote a long email to my boss.

items.nl: **Liep** jij vanochtend ook langs het kanaal?
items.en: Did you also walk along the canal this morning?
items.note: No -t for jij, not even in a question.

items.nl: Mijn ouders **waren** vorige week in Brugge.
items.en: My parents were in Bruges last week.

items.nl: **Was** u gisteren ook op de vergadering?
items.en: Were you at the meeting yesterday as well?
items.note: u was: the same form as ik and hij.

blocks.text: Spelling and sound in the plural

Because the plural adds -en, the normal spelling rules apply (see *Spelling: long and short vowels*). A long vowel written double is written single in the open syllable, and f becomes v, s becomes z: *schreef* → *schreven*, *koos* → *kozen*. A short vowel stays short, so the consonant is doubled: *won* → *wonnen*, *begon* → *begonnen*.

Watch the **a-verbs**: a short *a* in the singular becomes a **long a** in the plural, so it is written with one consonant: las → **lazen**, gaf → **gaven**, sprak → **spraken**, nam → **namen**, zat → **zaten**, at → **aten**. Exceptions: had → **hadden** keeps its short a, and was → **waren** changes s into r.
The most common strong verbs

Strong verbs fall into groups that share the same vowel change. Learning them in groups makes them much easier to remember. Verbs with a prefix change in the same way as the basic verb: *begrijpen* → *begreep*, *vertrekken* → *vertrok*, *opstaan* → *stond op*.

blocks.caption: ij → ee, and ie / ui → oo
i / e → o (short o: the consonant doubles in the plural)
→ a in the singular, long a in the plural

blocks.text: Irregular verbs

blocks.caption: Learn these by heart: they are among the most used words in Dutch

items: **willen**: *wilde* is the neutral form; *wou* is very common in speech (Ik **wou** je nog bellen). The plural is *wilden*.
**zeggen**: *zei – zeiden* is the usual form; *zegde – zegden* also exists but sounds formal (it is more common in Belgium).
**worden**: *hij werd*, *jij werd*: no -t, unlike the present *hij wordt*.
**kunnen** and **zullen** have a d in the plural: *wij konden*, *wij zouden*.
**-cht forms**: *denken, brengen, kopen, zoeken* and *mogen* all end in -cht: *dacht, bracht, kocht, zocht, mocht*.

items.nl: Vorige week **aten** we bij mijn ouders in Haarlem.
items.en: Last week we had dinner at my parents' in Haarlem.
He said nothing and went home.

items.nl: Toen ik klein was, **wilde** ik piloot worden.
items.en: When I was little, I wanted to be a pilot.
We couldn't find the address.

items.nl: Ze **kwam** te laat, want de trein **had** vertraging.
items.en: She was late because the train was delayed.

blocks.text: Mixed verbs

A few verbs mix the two systems. *Lachen*, *bakken*, *wassen* and *heten* have a regular past (*lachte, bakte, waste, heette*) but a strong participle (*gelachen, gebakken, gewassen, geheten*). *Vragen* and *zeggen* do the opposite: a strong or irregular past (*vroeg, zei*) but a regular participle (*gevraagd, gezegd*).
Separable verbs
In a main clause the prefix of a separable verb goes to the end, just as in the present (see *Separable verbs*). In a subordinate clause, prefix and verb are written together again at the end.

items.en: I got up at six this morning.

items.nl: De trein **kwam** tien minuten te laat **aan**.
items.en: The train arrived ten minutes late.
She didn't take her umbrella with her.

items.nl: Ik was moe omdat ik zo vroeg **opstond**.
items.en: I was tired because I got up so early.
items.note: Subordinate clause: prefix and verb together at the end.

blocks.why: In the simple past no -t is added for jij, u or hij: hij werd, jij werd. Only the present has hij wordt.
Lezen is a strong verb: it changes its vowel and never takes -de or -te.
The short a of las becomes a long a in the plural, so it is written with one consonant, and s becomes z: lazen.

blocks.text: Learn each strong verb as a set of four: infinitive, past singular, past plural and participle, for example *lezen – las – lazen – gelezen* or *schrijven – schreef – schreven – geschreven*. The participles are covered in *Perfect tense: irregular participles*.

lessons.title: Perfect or simple past?
lessons.summary: Choose between the perfect and the simple past when you talk or write about the past, and use toen and vroeger with the simple past.

blocks.text: Dutch has two everyday past tenses: the perfect (*Ik heb gewerkt*) and the simple past (*Ik werkte*). They can refer to exactly the same moment, and the choice does not follow English. *Ik heb hem gisteren gezien* is perfectly normal Dutch, although English says 'I saw him yesterday', never 'I have seen him yesterday'.

Use the **perfect** to report a single completed event or a piece of news, especially in conversation. Use the **simple past** to tell a story, to describe a situation or background in the past, for habits in the past, and after *toen* (when).

rows: news, a result that matters now
a story: one event after another
Hij **stond op**, **pakte** zijn tas en **ging** weg.
Toen ik in Leiden **woonde**, **fietste** ik overal naartoe.

blocks.text: In conversation: the perfect
When you tell someone what you did, the perfect is the default, even with time words like *gisteren*, *vorige week* or *in 2019*. Use it for one event or a short report of what happened.

items.en: What did you do at the weekend?

items.nl: Ik **heb** mijn oma **bezocht** en we **hebben** samen **gekookt**.
items.en: I visited my grandmother and we cooked together.
Have you ever been to Maastricht?

items.nl: Ik **heb** hem gisteren in de stad **gezien**.
items.en: I saw him in town yesterday.
items.note: Perfect with gisteren: normal in Dutch, impossible in English.

blocks.text: Stories and descriptions: the simple past

As soon as you tell a story with several events, or describe what a situation was like, Dutch switches to the simple past. Novels, news reports and fairy tales are written in it. A typical pattern: the first sentence uses the perfect to set the time frame, the details follow in the simple past, and a closing comment can return to the perfect.

items.en: I went to Amsterdam yesterday.
items.note: Perfect: sets the time frame.

items.nl: Het **was** heel druk in de stad.
items.en: It was very busy in town.
items.note: Simple past: description.

items.nl: We **liepen** eerst door het Vondelpark en daarna **gingen** we naar het Rijksmuseum.
items.en: First we walked through the Vondelpark and then we went to the Rijksmuseum.
items.note: Simple past: one event after another.

items.en: It was a lovely day.
items.note: Perfect: summing up.

blocks.text: Some verbs prefer the simple past even in conversation: **zijn**, **hebben** and the modal verbs. *Ik was ziek*, *Ik had geen tijd* and *Ik moest werken* sound more natural than the perfect. The same goes for *vinden* when you give your opinion: *Ik vond het leuk*.
Toen and vroeger

*Toen* at the start of a subordinate clause means 'when' for one moment or period in the past. It takes the simple past, with the verb at the end (see *Subordinate clauses: verb at the end*). In a main clause, *toen* means 'then' and is followed directly by the verb. *Vroeger* (in the past, used to) also calls for the simple past.

items.nl: **Toen** ik twaalf **was**, **kreeg** ik mijn eerste telefoon.
items.en: When I was twelve, I got my first phone.

items.nl: **Toen** de film **begon**, **zaten** we nog in de auto.
items.en: When the film started, we were still in the car.

items.nl: We aten eerst, en **toen gingen** we naar de bioscoop.
items.en: First we ate, and then we went to the cinema.
items.note: toen = then: the verb comes straight after it.

items.nl: **Vroeger fietste** ik elke dag naar school.
items.en: I used to cycle to school every day.

blocks.text: Still going on? Use the present

For something that started in the past and is **still true now**, Dutch uses the **present tense** with *al* or *sinds*, where English uses the present perfect: Ik **woon** hier al vijf jaar (I have lived here for five years).

items.nl: Ik **woon** al vijf jaar in Utrecht.
items.en: I have lived in Utrecht for five years.
items.note: And I still live there.

items.en: I lived in Utrecht for five years.
items.note: Finished: I no longer live there.

items.en: We have known each other since 2018.

blocks.wrong: Toen ik jong **ben geweest**, **heb** ik in Gent **gewoond**.
blocks.right: Toen ik jong **was**, **woonde** ik in Gent.
blocks.why: A toen-clause about a past situation takes the simple past, and the main clause that goes with it normally does too.
The situation is still going on, so Dutch uses the present tense with sinds or al. The perfect would mean you no longer live there.

blocks.text: Not sure? In speech, the perfect for single events plus the simple past of *zijn*, *hebben* and the modal verbs will almost always sound natural. In Belgium the perfect is used even more in speech; in writing, stories are told in the simple past everywhere.

lessons.title: The imperative
lessons.summary: Give instructions, requests, advice and warnings with the imperative, the polite u-form and the infinitive used as an instruction.

blocks.text: The imperative (*de gebiedende wijs*) tells someone to do something: an instruction, a request, advice or a warning. Dutch makes it very simply: take the stem of the verb and put it first. There is no subject.

Imperative = the **stem** of the verb (the ik-form of the present), at the start of the sentence: **Kom** binnen! **Wacht** even. The same form is used for one person and for a group (jij and jullie).

blocks.caption: The imperative is the stem, with the same spelling rules as the ik-form

blocks.text: Zijn and hebben
Two verbs are irregular. The imperative of *zijn* is **wees**, and the imperative of *hebben* is **heb**.

items.en: Be quiet, the baby is sleeping!
Don't be afraid.
Be patient, it will take a little longer.
Rest assured, everything will be fine.
items.note: The polite u-form of wees.

blocks.text: Polite requests
Polite imperative: **stem + t + u**: **Komt** u binnen. **Gaat** u zitten. For zijn: **Weest** u ... Without u, never add -t: **Kom** binnen! (not *Komt binnen!*).

The u-imperative is polite but direct; you hear it from shop staff, doctors and receptionists. A question with **Wilt u** or **Kunt u** + infinitive is softer. Adding *alstublieft* (to u) or *alsjeblieft* (to jij) makes any request more polite.

items.en: Come in, Mrs Jansen.
Please take a seat.
Would you sign here, please?
Could you close the window, please?
items.note: The informal version, with jij.

blocks.text: Separable and reflexive verbs

With a separable verb, the stem comes first and the prefix goes to the end of the sentence (see *Separable verbs*). Reflexive verbs keep their pronoun: *je* when you talk to jij, *u* or *zich* in the polite form (see *Reflexive verbs*).

items.en: Give me a call tomorrow.
Turn off the light when you leave.
Take an umbrella, it's going to rain.
Hurry up, the train is about to leave!
Please report to the reception desk.

blocks.text: Negative imperatives
*Niet* follows the normal rules (see *Negation: niet and geen*): after a definite object, but before an adjective, a place or a separable prefix. *Geen* replaces een or a noun without an article.

items.en: Don't do that!
Don't forget your keys.
Don't be so impatient.
Don't worry.
Don't be late tomorrow.

blocks.text: Softening words: even, maar, eens

A bare imperative can sound abrupt. Dutch speakers soften it with small words right after the verb: **even** (just, for a moment), **maar** (go ahead, feel free) and **eens** (just, why don't you). They are covered fully in *Modal particles* (B1).

items.en: Hang on a moment, I'm coming.
Come on in.
items.note: maar: permission or encouragement.

items.en: Have a look at what I found!

blocks.text: The infinitive as an instruction
On signs, in recipes and manuals, and in commands to a group, Dutch often uses the infinitive, at the end. It is impersonal: it addresses nobody in particular.

items.en: No smoking.
No parking here.
Peel the potatoes and cut them into pieces.
All aboard, please!
Pay attention, guys!

blocks.why: The imperative is the bare stem. A -t is only added in the polite form with u: Komt u binnen.
Zijn has a special imperative: wees.
Separable verbs split in the imperative: the stem comes first and the prefix goes to the end.

blocks.text: For a friendly instruction, add *even* or *maar* and *alsjeblieft*: *Doe even de deur dicht, alsjeblieft.* A bare *Doe de deur dicht!* sounds like an order.

lessons.title: The future: present tense, gaan and zullen
lessons.summary: Talk about the future with the present tense, gaan + infinitive and zullen + infinitive, and make offers and suggestions with Zal ik...? and Zullen we...?

blocks.text: Dutch has no single 'future tense'. There are three common ways to talk about the future, and the most frequent one is also the simplest: the present tense. *Gaan* + infinitive (see *The future with gaan*) is used for plans, and *zullen* + infinitive for promises, offers, suggestions and formal predictions.

Use the **present tense** with a time word for most future events. Use **gaan + infinitive** for plans and for things you can see coming. Use **zullen + infinitive** for promises, offers, suggestions and formal predictions.

rows: We **gaan** in de zomer een huis **kopen**.
We're going to buy a house this summer.
Kijk eens naar die wolken: het **gaat regenen**.
Look at those clouds: it's going to rain.
Shall we go to the beach?
Morgen **zal** het in het hele land droog **blijven**.
Tomorrow it will stay dry across the whole country.

blocks.text: The forms of zullen

blocks.caption: zullen is irregular in the singular; the past is zou, zouden (see Zou and zouden, B1)

blocks.text: Like a modal verb, *zullen* stands in second position and the infinitive goes to the end, without *te*. The same goes for *gaan*. In a subordinate clause both verbs go to the end (see *Subordinate clauses: verb at the end*).

items.en: I'll call you tomorrow.
items.note: A promise.

items.en: Tomorrow I'm going to tidy up the garden.

items.nl: Ik denk dat we volgend jaar **gaan verhuizen**.
items.en: I think we're going to move next year.
items.note: Subordinate clause: both verbs at the end.

items.nl: Hij belooft dat hij op tijd **zal komen**.
items.en: He promises that he'll be on time.

blocks.text: Offers and suggestions

*Zal ik ...?* offers to do something for someone (Shall I ...?). *Zullen we ...?* suggests doing something together (Shall we ...?). *Laten we* + infinitive is another way to make a suggestion: *Laten we gaan!* (Let's go!).

items.nl: **Zal** ik je even **helpen** met die tas?
items.en: Shall I help you with that bag?
Shall we have Chinese food tonight?
Shall we meet at eight?
Let's order a pizza.

blocks.text: Which one should I use?

In everyday speech the present tense is by far the most common: *Ik bel je morgen* (I'll call you tomorrow). *Zullen* for a plain future fact sounds formal or bookish, so use it mainly for promises, offers and suggestions, or in writing. *Gaan* points to a plan or decision: *Ik ga Spaans leren* (I'm going to learn Spanish).
English 'will' is not Dutch *wil*! *Ik wil komen* means 'I want to come'. 'I'll come' is *Ik kom* or *Ik zal komen*.
*Zullen* + *wel* can also express a guess about the present: *Hij zal wel ziek zijn* (He's probably ill). This use is covered in *Future perfect and zullen for probability* (B1).

blocks.why: Willen means 'to want'. For a prediction use gaan + infinitive, or simply the present: Morgen regent het.
Zullen and gaan are followed by a bare infinitive, without te.
The ik-form of zullen is zal. Zul only appears when jij follows the verb: Zul jij ...?

lessons.title: Diminutives
lessons.summary: Form diminutives with -je, -tje, -pje, -etje and -kje, use them as het-words with a plural in -s, and understand their different meanings.

blocks.text: Dutch uses the diminutive (*het verkleinwoord*) all the time. You add an ending to a noun to make it small, sweet or casual: *het huis* → *het huisje* (the little house), *de kop* → *het kopje* (the cup). The basic ending is -je, but depending on how the noun ends, it becomes -tje, -pje, -etje or -kje.
Every diminutive is a **het**-word, whatever the article of the original noun: *de stoel* → **het stoeltje**. The plural always ends in **-s**: *de stoeltjes*.
Which ending?

blocks.caption: The ending depends on the last sounds of the noun
rows: after most consonants, such as p, t, k, f, s, ch and d
after a vowel or diphthong; a final a, o or u is doubled
ei → **eitje**, koe → **koetje**, trui → **truitje**, auto → **autootje**, oma → **omaatje**, menu → **menuutje**
after l, n, r or w with a long vowel, a diphthong or an unstressed syllable before it
stoel → **stoeltje**, deur → **deurtje**, tuin → **tuintje**, vrouw → **vrouwtje**, tafel → **tafeltje**, keuken → **keukentje**, kamer → **kamertje**
after m with a long vowel, a diphthong, an unstressed syllable, l or r before it
boom → **boompje**, raam → **raampje**, duim → **duimpje**, bezem → **bezempje**, film → **filmpje**, arm → **armpje**
after l, m, n, r or ng with a short, stressed vowel before it; the consonant is doubled (not ng)
bal → **balletje**, kam → **kammetje**, pan → **pannetje**, ster → **sterretje**, ring → **ringetje**, ding → **dingetje**

blocks.text: Two spelling points. A final a, o or u is a long vowel, so it is doubled before -tje to stay long: *autootje*, *omaatje*, *menuutje*. After a short vowel, the consonant is doubled before -etje, just as in the plural: *bal* → *ballen* → *balletje*.

items.nl: We wonen in een klein **huisje** aan de rand van Delft.
items.en: We live in a little house on the edge of Delft.

items.nl: Mijn opa rijdt nog in een oud **autootje**.
items.en: My grandad still drives a little old car.

items.nl: De kinderen spelen met een **balletje** in de tuin.
items.en: The children are playing with a ball in the garden.

items.nl: Op het balkon staat een **boompje** in een pot.
items.en: There's a little tree in a pot on the balcony.

items.nl: Er was eens een **koninkje** in een ver land.
items.en: Once upon a time there was a little king in a faraway land.
That test? It was a piece of cake!
items.note: een eitje (a little egg) also means 'something very easy'.

blocks.text: Always het, plural -s

Because every diminutive is a het-word, everything around it follows het: *het*, *dit* and *dat*, *ons*, the relative pronoun *dat*, and the adjective without -e after een (see *Adjective endings: when to add -e*). In the plural it takes *de*, like every plural.

items.en: The little chair is in the children's room.
This little dog belongs to my neighbours.
She has a sweet kitten.
items.note: het katje: no -e on the adjective after een.

items.en: Our little garden is small but cosy.

items.nl: **De huisjes** aan het water zijn erg duur.
items.en: The little houses by the water are very expensive.

blocks.text: A few special forms

items: Some nouns with a short vowel get a **long** vowel: het glas → het **glaasje**, het blad → het **blaadje**, het schip → het **scheepje**, het gat → het **gaatje**.
de jongen → het **jongetje** (not *jongentje*).
A few nouns ending in -b or -g also take -etje: de brug → het **bruggetje**, de vlag → het **vlaggetje**.

Some words are nearly always used as diminutives and have their own meaning: het **meisje** (girl), het **koekje** (biscuit), het **broodje** (bread roll, sandwich), het **kaartje** (ticket), het **toetje** (dessert), het **sprookje** (fairy tale).
Some adverbs have a diminutive form in -jes: **zachtjes** (softly), **netjes** (neatly), **eventjes** (just for a moment).

blocks.text: What diminutives mean

rows: a little house by the sea
a beer, a day out, an hour or so
een **kopje** koffie, een **stukje** taart, een **glaasje** water
a cup of coffee, a piece of cake, a glass of water
a little job (nothing important), a little man

blocks.text: In Belgium you will often hear diminutives in -ke in informal speech (*een boekske*, *Manneken Pis*). In writing, standard Dutch uses the -je endings everywhere.

blocks.why: All diminutives are het-words, even when the original noun is a de-word (de stoel).
After a vowel the ending is -tje, and a final a, o or u is doubled to keep it long: autootje.
Nouns ending in unstressed -ing change -ing into -inkje: koning → koninkje.

lessons.title: Joining main clauses: en, maar, of, want, dus
lessons.summary: Join two main clauses with en, maar, of, want and dus, keeping normal word order, and know when to use want and when omdat.

blocks.text: To join two complete sentences (main clauses), Dutch uses the coordinating conjunctions *en* (and), *maar* (but), *of* (or), *want* (because) and *dus* (so). They are easy to use, because they do not change the word order of the clause that follows.

**En**, **maar**, **of** and **want** stand outside the clause, in 'position 0'. After them the clause has normal main-clause order: position 1 (usually the subject), then the finite verb in position 2: Ik blijf thuis, **want** ik **ben** ziek.

rows: Ik kook **en** mijn vriend doet de afwas.
I cook and my boyfriend does the dishes.
Ik wil graag komen, **maar** ik heb geen tijd.
I'd love to come, but I don't have time.
Gaan we met de trein, **of** nemen we de auto?
Are we going by train, or are we taking the car?
Ik neem een jas mee, **want** het is koud.
I'm taking a coat, because it's cold.
Het regent, **dus** ik neem de bus.
It's raining, so I'll take the bus.

blocks.caption: The conjunction does not count: the verb is still the second element after it

blocks.text: Look at the last line: if something other than the subject comes first after the conjunction, you get inversion, exactly as in any main clause. It is *morgen* that causes it, not *en*.

items.nl: Ik ben moe, **want** gisteren **heb** ik tot laat gewerkt.
items.en: I'm tired, because yesterday I worked until late.

items.nl: Ze spreekt goed Nederlands, **maar** ze **schrijft** het niet zo goed.
items.en: She speaks Dutch well, but she doesn't write it so well.
Would you like coffee or tea?
items.note: En and of can also join single words.

items.nl: Ik kom thuis **en** ga meteen naar bed.
items.en: I get home and go straight to bed.
items.note: Same subject: it can be left out after en and maar.

blocks.text: dus: two possible word orders

**Dus** can be used like *en*, in position 0 with normal order, or in position 1, followed directly by the verb. Both are correct: Het regent, **dus ik neem** de bus. Het regent, **dus neem ik** de bus.
*Dus* can also stand later in the clause, like an ordinary adverb: *Ik neem **dus** de bus* (So I'm taking the bus). What *dus* never does is send the verb to the end.
want or omdat?

*Want* and *omdat* both mean 'because', but *omdat* starts a subordinate clause, with the verb at the end (see *Subordinate clauses: verb at the end*). A want-clause always follows the main clause; an omdat-clause can also come first.

rows: subordinate clause: verb at the end
at the start of the sentence?
possible: Omdat ik ziek **ben**, **blijf** ik thuis.
yes: Hij is thuis, want zijn fiets staat er.

items.en: I'm staying at home, because I'm ill.
I'm staying at home because I'm ill.
Because I'm ill, I'm staying at home.

items.nl: Het heeft geregend, **want** de straat is nat.
items.en: It has rained, because (I can see that) the street is wet.
items.note: Only want: the wet street is your evidence, not the cause of the rain.

blocks.text: of = or, of = whether

Between two main clauses, *of* means 'or' and does not change the word order. Don't confuse it with *of* meaning 'whether, if', which starts a subordinate clause with the verb at the end: *Ik weet niet **of** hij **komt**.*
Commas: put a comma before *maar*, *want* and *dus* when they join two clauses. Before *en* and *of* the comma is usually left out, unless the sentence is long or would otherwise be unclear.

blocks.wrong: Ik blijf thuis, want ik ziek **ben**.
blocks.right: Ik blijf thuis, want ik **ben** ziek.
blocks.why: Want is followed by a normal main clause, with the verb in second place. Only omdat sends the verb to the end.

blocks.wrong: **Want** het regent, ik neem de bus.
blocks.why: A want-clause can never come first. To start with the reason, use omdat; the main clause then starts with its verb.

blocks.wrong: Ik ben moe en **ga ik** naar bed.
blocks.right: Ik ben moe en **ik ga** naar bed.
blocks.why: En does not cause inversion: after en the subject comes first, then the verb. You may also leave out the repeated subject: en ga naar bed.

lessons.title: Subordinate clauses: verb at the end
lessons.summary: Build subordinate clauses with dat, omdat, als, toen and other conjunctions, put the finite verb at the end, and start the main clause with its verb when the subordinate clause comes first.

blocks.text: A subordinate clause (*de bijzin*) cannot stand on its own: it depends on a main clause. It starts with a subordinating conjunction such as *dat* (that), *omdat* (because) or *als* (if, when). The big difference with English: in a subordinate clause the finite verb moves to the very end.
Subordinate clause order: **conjunction + subject + everything else + finite verb**. Ik denk **dat** hij morgen **komt**. Ik blijf thuis **omdat** ik ziek **ben**.
The most common conjunctions

rows: Ze is blij **omdat** ze een nieuwe baan **heeft**.
**Wanneer** ik in Gent **ben**, bezoek ik mijn tante.
when (one moment or period in the past)
**Toen** ik klein **was**, woonde ik in Zwolle.
Ik luister naar de radio **terwijl** ik **kook**.

blocks.text: *Als* is the everyday word for both 'if' and 'when' in the present, the future or for something that happens repeatedly. For one specific moment or period in the past, use *toen*. *Wanneer* is a slightly more formal 'when, whenever' and is also the question word 'when?'. 'If' in the sense of 'whether' is always *of*, never *als*.
Subordinate clause first: the main clause starts with its verb
A subordinate clause at the start of the sentence fills **position 1**. The main clause therefore continues with its **finite verb**, followed by the subject: **Als** het regent, **blijf** ik thuis.
Remember the pattern **verb, verb**: *Als het regent, blijf ik thuis.* The last word before the comma is a verb, and the first word after it is a verb too.
Verb groups at the end

When a subordinate clause has more than one verb, they all go to the end. With a modal verb or *gaan* + infinitive, the finite verb usually comes first: *dat ik kan komen*. With the perfect, both orders are correct: *dat hij heeft gewerkt* and *dat hij gewerkt heeft*. A separable verb is written as one word at the end: *omdat ik vroeg opsta*. More in *Verb clusters in subordinate clauses* (B1).

items.nl: Ik denk dat ik morgen **kan komen**.
items.en: I think I can come tomorrow.

items.nl: Ze zegt dat ze ziek **is geweest**.
items.en: She says she has been ill.
items.note: Also correct: dat ze ziek geweest is.

items.nl: Weet je of hij al **heeft gebeld**?
items.en: Do you know if he has called yet?
items.note: Also correct: of hij al gebeld heeft.

items.en: Give me a call when you arrive.
items.note: The separable verb aankomen is written as one word again.

items.nl: Ik bel je als ik morgen **niet kan komen**.
items.en: I'll call you if I can't come tomorrow.
items.note: niet comes before the verbs at the end.

blocks.text: Everything in the middle keeps the order it has in a main clause: time before manner before place, and *niet* before the verbs at the end (see *Word order in the middle: time, manner, place and niet*).

blocks.why: In a subordinate clause the finite verb goes to the end, unlike in English.
The subordinate clause fills position 1, so the main clause must continue with its verb.
English 'if' meaning 'whether' is of in Dutch. Als means 'if' only as a condition.

lessons.title: om ... te + infinitive
lessons.summary: Say why you do something with om ... te + infinitive, use the same structure after adjectives and nouns such as leuk, tijd and zin, and handle separable verbs inside it.

blocks.text: English uses 'to' or 'in order to' to say why you do something: 'I'm going to the shop to buy bread.' Dutch uses a two-part structure: **om** at the start and **te** + infinitive at the very end. Everything else goes in between.
Purpose: **om** + (object, time, place ...) + **te + infinitive** at the end. Ik ga naar de winkel **om** brood **te kopen**.

items.nl: Ik ga naar de bakker **om** brood **te kopen**.
items.en: I'm going to the baker's to buy bread.

items.nl: We sparen **om** volgend jaar naar Canada **te gaan**.
items.en: We're saving up to go to Canada next year.

items.nl: Hij volgt een cursus **om** zijn Nederlands **te verbeteren**.
items.en: He's taking a course to improve his Dutch.

items.nl: **Om** fit **te blijven**, **fietst** ze elke dag naar haar werk.
items.en: To stay fit, she cycles to work every day.
items.note: om-clause first: the main clause continues with its verb.

blocks.text: Separable verbs
With a separable verb, **te** goes between the prefix and the verb, written as three separate words: opbellen → **op te bellen**, meegaan → **mee te gaan**, uitrusten → **uit te rusten**.

items.nl: Ik heb geen tijd **om** je **op te bellen**.
items.en: I don't have time to call you.

items.nl: Heb je zin **om mee te gaan**?
items.en: Do you feel like coming along?

items.nl: Ze gaat even zitten **om uit te rusten**.
items.en: She sits down for a moment to rest.

blocks.text: After adjectives and nouns

The same structure completes many adjectives and nouns. Typical patterns are *Het is* + adjective + *om te*, and nouns such as *tijd*, *zin*, *geld*, *plan*, *idee* and *kans*. After an adjective, formal Dutch sometimes leaves out *om* (*Het is belangrijk goed te slapen*), but with *om* it is always correct.

rows: Het is leuk **om** in de zee **te zwemmen**.
It's fun to swim in the sea.
It's important to get enough sleep.
Dit boek is moeilijk **om te lezen**.
This book is difficult to read.
Ik heb geen tijd **om te koken**.
I don't have time to cook.
Heb je zin **om** vanavond uit eten **te gaan**?
Do you feel like going out for dinner tonight?
We hebben geen geld **om** een auto **te kopen**.
We don't have the money to buy a car.
Ze heeft het plan **om** naar Spanje **te verhuizen**.
She plans to move to Spain.
Het is tijd **om** naar huis **te gaan**.

blocks.text: niet and modal verbs inside the om-clause
*Niet* goes just before the part it negates, usually right before *te*. A modal verb can also follow *te*, with its own infinitive after it.

items.nl: Ik vertrek vroeg **om niet** te laat **te komen**.
items.en: I'm leaving early so as not to be late.
items.note: te laat = too late; the second te belongs to the infinitive.

items.nl: Ze leert Nederlands **om** hier **te kunnen werken**.
items.en: She's learning Dutch to be able to work here.

blocks.text: Same subject

An om-clause has no subject of its own: the person doing the action is the **subject of the main clause** (or people in general after *Het is ... om te*). If the subject is different, use **zodat** + a subordinate clause: Ik praat langzaam, **zodat** jij het **begrijpt**.

items.nl: Ik bel de dokter **om** een afspraak **te maken**.
items.en: I'm calling the doctor to make an appointment.
items.note: I call and I make the appointment.

items.nl: Ik leg het nog een keer uit, **zodat** iedereen het **begrijpt**.
items.en: I'll explain it once more so that everyone understands.
items.note: Different subject: zodat.

blocks.text: No om ... te after modal verbs

English 'to' after 'want', 'have to' or 'be able to' is not translated: modal verbs take a bare infinitive (see *Modal verbs: kunnen, willen, moeten, mogen*). Some other verbs, such as *proberen* and *beginnen*, take *te* + infinitive, usually without *om* (see *Verbs with te + infinitive*, B1).

blocks.wrong: Ik ga naar de winkel **voor** brood **te kopen**.
blocks.right: Ik ga naar de winkel **om** brood **te kopen**.
blocks.why: Purpose is expressed with om ... te. 'Voor ... te' is heard in informal Belgian Dutch, but it is not standard.

blocks.wrong: Ik heb geen tijd om je **te opbellen**.
blocks.right: Ik heb geen tijd om je **op te bellen**.
blocks.why: With separable verbs, te goes between the prefix and the verb.
Modal verbs like willen take a bare infinitive, without om and without te.

blocks.wrong: Ik praat langzaam **om** jij het **te begrijpen**.
blocks.why: An om-clause cannot have its own subject. When the subject is different, use zodat.

lessons.title: Word order in the middle: time, manner, place and niet
lessons.summary: Put time, manner and place in the right order, place object pronouns early and put niet in the right spot in the middle of a Dutch sentence.

blocks.text: In a main clause the finite verb is in position 2, and infinitives, participles and separable prefixes go to the end (see *Word order: the verb in second place*). Everything else goes in between, in the 'middle field' (*het middenveld*). The order there is fairly fixed, and it is often the reverse of English.
In the middle of the sentence the order is **time – manner – place**: when? – how? – where (to)? Ik ga **morgen** **met de trein** **naar Gent**.

English usually has the opposite order: 'I'm going to Ghent by train tomorrow' (place – manner – time). In Dutch the place, especially a destination with *naar*, comes last, just before any verbs at the end.

items.nl: Ik ga **morgen met de trein naar Gent**.
items.en: I'm going to Ghent by train tomorrow.

items.nl: Hij komt **elke dag met de fiets naar school**.
items.en: He comes to school by bike every day.

items.nl: We hebben **gisteren gezellig in de tuin** gegeten.
items.en: We had a nice meal in the garden yesterday.

items.nl: **Volgende week** ga ik **met mijn zus naar Antwerpen**.
items.en: Next week I'm going to Antwerp with my sister.
items.note: Time in position 1; the rest keeps its order.

blocks.text: Any part can move to position 1 for emphasis, most often the time. The parts that stay in the middle keep their order: *Morgen ga ik met de trein naar Gent.*
Pronouns come early

Unstressed object pronouns (*me, je, hem, haar, het, ons, ze*) and *zich* come **right after the finite verb**, or right after the subject if the subject follows the verb, and **before** time words. A noun with *een* comes after the time: Ik heb **het** gisteren gekocht. Ik heb gisteren **een fiets** gekocht.

items.nl: Ik heb **hem** gisteren in de stad gezien.
items.en: I saw him in town yesterday.
I'll give it back to you tomorrow.
items.note: Two pronouns: het comes first.

items.nl: Ik heb gisteren **een nieuwe jas** gekocht.
items.en: I bought a new coat yesterday.
items.note: Indefinite noun: after the time.

items.en: I bought the coat yesterday.
items.note: A definite noun may also come before the time.

items.en: She made a mistake this morning.

blocks.text: Where does niet go?

The basics are in *Negation: niet and geen*. When *niet* negates the whole sentence, its place depends on what else is in the middle. Think of two groups: parts that come **before** *niet* and parts that come **after** it.

*Niet* comes **after** object pronouns, definite objects and time words like *morgen*, *vandaag* and *nu*. It comes **before** manner, place and direction, most prepositional phrases, adjectives and nouns after *zijn* or *worden*, and the verbs and separable prefixes at the end.

rows: definite objects: Ik ken **die man niet**.
place and direction: Ik ga **niet naar huis**.
prepositional phrases: Ik wacht **niet op de bus**.
predicate adjectives: Het huis is **niet groot**.
verbs and prefixes at the end: Ik heb **niet gewerkt**. Ik bel je **niet op**.
vaak, altijd, lang: Ze is **niet vaak** thuis.

items.nl: Ik heb het boek gisteren **niet** gelezen.
items.en: I didn't read the book yesterday.

items.nl: We gaan morgen **niet** met de auto naar Gent.
items.en: We're not going to Ghent by car tomorrow.
items.note: niet after the time, before manner and place.

items.en: He won't be on time today.
I won't call you tonight.

blocks.text: *Niet* can also go directly before one specific part to contrast it with something else, usually followed by *maar*: *Ik ga **niet morgen**, maar overmorgen.* More on this in *Negation in more detail* (B1).

blocks.wrong: Ik ga naar Gent morgen met de trein.
blocks.right: Ik ga morgen met de trein naar Gent.
blocks.why: The Dutch order is time – manner – place, the reverse of English.
Unstressed pronouns like het, hem and haar come early, before time words.
When niet negates the whole sentence, it follows a definite object.
Niet goes before a place or direction.

exercises.prompt: Onze buren zijn erg ___. (aardig)
exercises.explanation: After a verb like zijn the adjective is not followed by a noun, so it never gets an ending: zijn erg aardig.

exercises.prompt: Ik zie een ___ huis.
exercises.explanation: After een, an adjective before a het-word gets no -e: een mooi huis. Huis is a het-word.

exercises.prompt: De ___ auto staat voor de deur.
exercises.explanation: After the definite article de, the adjective always gets -e: de rode auto. Note the spelling change from rood to rode.

exercises.prompt: Wij drinken ___ koffie.
exercises.explanation: Koffie is a de-word, and adjectives before de-words get -e even without an article: warme koffie.

exercises.prompt: Het ___ meisje speelt buiten.
exercises.explanation: After the definite article het, the adjective gets -e even before a het-word: het kleine meisje. Only a singular het-word without a definite word in front (een klein meisje) drops the -e.

exercises.prompt: Hebben jullie ons ___ huis al gezien? (nieuw)
exercises.explanation: Ons is a possessive, which counts as a definite word, so the adjective gets -e even before the het-word huis: ons nieuwe huis.

exercises.prompt: Wat een ___ kat! (dik)
exercises.explanation: Kat is a de-word, so the adjective gets -e. Dik has a short i, so the k is doubled to keep the vowel short: dikke.

exercises.prompt: Ze hebben een ___ tafel in de keuken. (made of wood)
exercises.explanation: Material adjectives ending in -en, such as houten, gouden and wollen, never take an extra -e: een houten tafel.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
choices: Ik heb een nieuw fiets en een nieuwe huis.
Ik heb een nieuwe fiets en een nieuw huis.
Ik heb een nieuwe fiets en een nieuwe huis.
Ik heb een nieuw fiets en een nieuw huis.
exercises.explanation: Fiets is a de-word, so it takes nieuwe. Huis is a het-word, and after een a singular het-word drops the -e: een nieuw huis.

exercises.prompt: Mijn broer is twee jaar ouder ___ ik.
exercises.explanation: After a comparative (ouder) Dutch uses dan: ouder dan ik. Als is used with zo … als for equal comparisons.

exercises.prompt: Deze fiets is ___ dan die fiets.
exercises.explanation: Duur ends in -r, so the comparative ending is -der: duurder. Dutch does not use meer with adjectives like this.

exercises.prompt: Dit boek is ___ dan dat boek.
exercises.explanation: Goed has an irregular comparative: beter. The form goeder does not exist in standard Dutch.

exercises.prompt: In de stad is een fiets vaak net zo snel ___ een auto.
exercises.explanation: Equal comparisons use (net) zo … als: net zo snel als een auto. Dan only follows a comparative such as sneller.

exercises.prompt: Ik heb deze week ___ tijd dan vorige week. (weinig)
exercises.explanation: Weinig is irregular: weinig – minder – minst. With dan you need the comparative: minder tijd.

exercises.prompt: Amsterdam is de ___ stad van Nederland.
exercises.explanation: The superlative is formed with -st: grootst. Before a noun after de it also gets the adjective ending -e: de grootste stad.

exercises.prompt: Dit is het ___ restaurant van de stad. (goed)
exercises.explanation: The superlative of goed is best. Before a noun, after het, it takes -e: het beste restaurant.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct translation: 'Tom works the hardest.'
exercises.explanation: When a superlative describes an action rather than a noun, Dutch uses het + superlative: het hardst.

exercises.prompt: Ons appartement is te klein. We zoeken een ___ huis. (groot)
exercises.explanation: The comparative of groot is groter. Huis is a het-word after een, so, like any adjective, it gets no -e: een groter huis.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct translation: 'I like reading.'
exercises.explanation: To say you like doing something, conjugate the verb normally and add graag after it: Ik lees graag.

exercises.prompt: Ik hou ___ Italiaans eten.
exercises.explanation: Houden in the meaning 'love, like' always goes with van: houden van.

exercises.prompt: Ik vind deze soep heel ___.
exercises.explanation: To say you like the taste of food or drink, use lekker vinden: Ik vind deze soep lekker. Graag and liever go with a verb of activity, not with vinden.

exercises.prompt: Ik drink ___ thee dan koffie.
exercises.explanation: Dan signals a comparison, so you need the comparative of graag, which is liever: liever thee dan koffie.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
choices: In de zomer ik zwem graag in zee.
In de zomer zwem ik graag in zee.
In de zomer zwem graag ik in zee.
In de zomer graag zwem ik in zee.
exercises.explanation: The sentence starts with In de zomer, so the verb comes second and the subject follows it (inversion). Graag comes after the subject: zwem ik graag.

exercises.prompt: Van alle sporten speel ik ___ tennis.
exercises.explanation: Van alle sporten asks for the superlative of graag, which is het liefst: what you like most of all.

exercises.prompt: Which is the correct polite request in a café?
choices: Ik graag wil een kopje thee.
Ik houd van een kopje thee.
Ik wil een kopje thee liefst.
Ik wil graag een kopje thee.
exercises.explanation: Polite requests use willen + graag, with the verb wil in second place and graag right after it: Ik wil graag een kopje thee.

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct translation: 'I don't like getting up early.'
choices: Ik sta graag niet vroeg op.
Ik niet graag sta vroeg op.
Ik sta niet graag vroeg op.
exercises.explanation: Not liking something is niet graag, placed after the verb: Ik sta niet graag vroeg op. Graag niet would mean you like not doing it.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence is correct?
exercises.explanation: Opbellen is separable: the conjugated part bel stays in second position and the prefix op goes to the very end of the main clause.

exercises.prompt: Ik ___ elke dag om zeven uur op.
exercises.explanation: Opstaan is a separable verb: in a main clause the prefix op moves to the end of the sentence. Only the stem sta fills the gap because op is already at the end.

exercises.prompt: De trein ___ om 10.15 uur in Utrecht aan. (aankomen)
exercises.explanation: In a main clause only komt goes to second position; the prefix aan is already at the end of the sentence.

exercises.prompt: Zij heeft haar moeder gisteren ___.
